blocks.text: Te khalu nava yogino mṛdu-madhya-adhimātra-upāyā 624 bhavanti I Tad yathā-- mṛdu- upāyo madhya-upāyo'dhimātra-upāya iti I Tatra mṛdu-upāyo'pi 625 tri-vidhaḥ-- mṛdu- saṃvego madhya-saṃvegas tīvra-saṃvega iti I Tathā madhya-upāyas tathā adhimātra- upāya iti I These yogis are of nine kinds according to whether their means, i.e., their method, are mild, moderate, or extreme; that is to say, there are mṛdūpāya [yogis] “(adherents) of the mild method,” madhyopāya [yogis] “(adherents) of the moderate method,” and adhimātropāya [yogis] “(adherents) of the extreme method.” And the mild method is also of three kinds according to whether the [yogi’s] drive is mild, moderate, or intense. And this also holds true for the moderate method and the extreme method.
Tatra_adhimātra-upāyānām 626 Among these [different varieties of yogis], for the adherents of the extreme method, that is to say,
“For those whose drive is intense, [samādhi] is near.” 627
The attainment of mental enstasis and the fruit of this enstasis are [near for those whose drive is intense]. /21/
624 MAAS 2006a: 32 reads amī instead of mṛdu...upāyā.
626 Vijñāna Bhikṣu considers that the word adhimātropāyānām is part of the sūtra, whereas, before him, Vācaspati rejected this reading.
627 BRONKHORST 1985 uses these three sūtra to support the hypothesis of a Patañjali who was both the sūtrakāra and the bhāṣyakāra.
